title: Decision-Making Fundamentals Circuit
objective: Assess and reinforce the fundamental decision-making behaviours introduced in DM-001 to DM-009 through a progressive multi-station circuit.
groundSize: Four stations using approximately half a ground.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Create four stations:
Station 1 – Scan and Receive: Players identify a visual cue before receiving.
Station 2 – Space and Pressure: Players lead into free space and react to a closing defender.
Station 3 – Option and Risk: Players select between safe, attacking and switch options.
Station 4 – Numbers and Field Position: Small-sided play begins with changing numbers and nominated field zones.
Divide the squad evenly between stations. Assign a coach or leader to each station where possible.
howTheDrillWorks:
Players complete four minutes of work at each station.
Station 1 scores scanning timing, body position and clean possession.
Station 2 scores space recognition and correct response to pressure.
Station 3 scores option selection and risk awareness.
Station 4 scores recognition of numerical advantage and field-position context.
Players receive one point for an appropriate decision and one point for successful execution.
Rotate after four minutes with one minute for explanation and movement.
Complete two circuits if time allows.
In the second circuit, increase pressure or reduce decision time.
Finish with a brief review of the most common team strengths and errors.
coachingPoints: Gather information before possession whenever possible.
Scan space, teammates, opponents and pressure sources.
Make the decision before perfect execution is demanded.
Recognise that the best option changes with field position and numbers.
Take attacking opportunities when the advantage is clear.
Retain possession when the risk is greater than the likely reward.
Re-scan after every disposal and turnover.
Separate decision quality from execution when assessing players.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether scanning occurs before possession.
Whether players identify useful space.
Whether decisions change appropriately under pressure.
Whether players select options that support the next phase.
Whether risk is adjusted to field position.
Whether players recognise numerical advantage.
Whether execution errors occur despite correct decisions.
Whether the same decision errors repeat across multiple stations.

commonErrors.error: Players focus only on completing the skill.
commonErrors.correction: Score decision quality separately from execution quality.

commonErrors.error: Scanning disappears when pressure increases.
commonErrors.correction: Reduce speed briefly and rebuild the pre-possession habit.

commonErrors.error: Players use the same option regardless of the picture.
commonErrors.correction: Change cues, defender positions and numerical situations frequently.

commonErrors.error: Players become overly conservative.
commonErrors.correction: Reward correct attacking decisions even when execution is imperfect.

commonErrors.error: Coaches provide the answer before the player decides.
commonErrors.correction: Use questioning after the action rather than directing during it.

commonErrors.error: Station rotations become disorganised.
commonErrors.correction: Use fixed groups, clear rotation direction and visible station numbers.

progressions: Remove verbal cues and rely on live information.
Increase defensive pressure.
Add scoreboard and time scenarios.
Connect all four stations into one continuous transition activity.
Ask players to self-assess and explain selected decisions.
Record individual decision scores across repeated sessions.
regressions: Run two stations at a time.
Allow a brief pause before possession.
Demonstrate the preferred scanning pattern at each station.
Remove scoring and focus on one decision behaviour per rotation.
successIndicators: Explain why a selected decision was appropriate.
Maintain decision quality as pressure increases.
matchApplication: The circuit brings together the core information-processing demands of Australian football. Players must scan, interpret space and pressure, assess risk, recognise numbers and choose an action that suits the position and phase of play.

title: Fundamental Decisions Assessment
objective: Assess players’ ability to apply the fundamental decision-making behaviours developed through DM-011 to DM-019 in a continuous, variable training activity.
groundSize: Half ground divided into a defensive start zone, midfield decision zone and attacking finish zone.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert scenarios with multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Divide the squad into two teams.
Create three connected zones.
The defensive start zone contains boundary, corridor and reset options.
The midfield zone contains changing numerical situations and potential switch opportunities.
The attacking zone contains marking targets and a scoring gate.
Coaches position spare footballs around the ground to create imperfect-possession restarts.
Use controlled pressure initially, increasing intensity as the activity develops.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacking team begins with possession in the defensive start zone.
Players must choose between the boundary, corridor or reset according to the defensive shape.
On entering the midfield zone, the coach releases an additional player to create either an attacking advantage, even numbers or a temporary disadvantage.
The team must recognise whether to continue forward, switch sides or retain possession.
A marked possession in the attacking zone requires an immediate play-on, hold or set-disposal decision.
At selected moments, the coach introduces an imperfect football to create broken play.
The attacking team scores one point for each correct decision and three points for completing the possession with a goal or target entry.
The defending team scores two points for forcing a poor decision and three for a turnover that produces a successful counterattack.
After a turnover, teams immediately reverse direction.
Play in four-minute blocks with one-minute review periods.
Rotate starting positions so all players experience different field zones.
Complete at least four blocks before recording assessment outcomes.
coachingPoints: Scan forward, wide and behind the football before possession.
Select receiving shape according to pressure.
Release immediately when the next target is ready.
Secure and rebalance when the disposal lane is not yet clear.
Confirm communicated options visually.
Play on after a mark only when a genuine advantage exists.
Use the switch when the ball side is overloaded.
Reassess immediately after fumbles, smothers and deflections.
Judge the decision separately from the execution result.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether players scan before receiving.
Whether they identify forward options without forcing play.
Whether receiving orientation matches the pressure source.
Whether release tempo suits target readiness.
Whether communication is visually confirmed.
Whether post-mark decisions create or preserve advantage.
Whether teams recognise overloaded and open sides.
Whether players recover mentally after errors.
Whether field position changes the selected risk.
Whether decision quality is maintained as fatigue increases.

commonErrors.error: Players revert to predetermined patterns.
commonErrors.correction: Change defensive positioning and starting numbers between repetitions.

commonErrors.error: Coaches judge only whether the disposal was completed.
commonErrors.correction: Record decision quality and execution quality as separate scores.

commonErrors.error: Players become overly conservative under assessment.
commonErrors.correction: Reward appropriate attacking decisions even when execution fails.

commonErrors.error: Scanning decreases as fatigue increases.
commonErrors.correction: Reduce the duration of blocks while maintaining decision complexity.

commonErrors.error: Teams fail to react after an error or turnover.
commonErrors.correction: Award transition points during the first five seconds after possession changes.

commonErrors.error: Players depend on coach instructions.
commonErrors.correction: Use review questions between blocks rather than directing every live action.

progressions: Increase defensive pressure to match intensity.
Remove marked channels and gates.
Add scoreboard and time scenarios.
Require nominated players to provide on-field leadership calls.
Record individual decision profiles across several sessions.
Begin from stoppages, kick-ins and turnover situations.
regressions: Assess one zone at a time.
Reduce the number of changing variables.
Allow a brief freeze before selected decisions.
Use smaller teams and shorter playing blocks.
Provide a single coaching focus for each player.
successIndicators: Select body orientation according to pressure.
Match release tempo to the situation.
Recognise when to switch or reset.
Adjust risk to field position and numerical balance.
Explain the reasoning behind their decisions.
matchApplication: The assessment recreates the changing information players process across a complete phase of Australian football. It connects defensive exit choices, midfield numbers, switching play, post-mark decisions and broken-play recovery in a continuous environment where the correct option changes from moment to moment.
relatedDrills: DM-015 – Mark, Play On or Hold

title: Receive, Run Through or Roll Out
objective: Teach players to decide whether to continue running through the receiving lane, roll away from pressure or stop and release immediately after taking possession.
coachingDifficulty: 3 – Intermediate organisation, rotations or several behaviours
setup:
Position a feeder at one end.
Place a receiver 12 metres away.
Set a continuation gate behind the receiver.
Mark a curved roll-out gate to one side.
Position one short-release target near the receive point.
A defender begins behind, beside or in front of the receiver.
howTheDrillWorks:
The receiver scans the defender before leading.
The feeder disposes to the receiver.
If the defender trails, the receiver continues running through the forward gate.
If the defender closes from the front, the receiver rolls away through the side gate.
If the defender arrives from the side and removes both movement lanes, the receiver releases immediately to support.
The receiver completes the next disposal after exiting.
One point is awarded for the correct movement choice.
One point is awarded for clean execution.
Rotate all roles after each repetition.
coachingPoints: Scan the defender’s starting position and movement.
Receive at speed when the forward lane is safe.
Roll towards space, not merely away from contact.
Use the body to protect the football.
Release immediately when movement lanes are closed.
Keep the feet active during possession.
Prepare the disposal before completing the turn.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether scanning occurs before possession.
Whether the receiver maintains momentum when unpressured.
Whether the roll-out moves away from the defender.
Whether players stop unnecessarily.
Whether the quick-release option is used when required.
Whether the football remains secure.

commonErrors.error: Receiver stops after every possession.
commonErrors.correction: Deliver the football into the running path and reward continuation.

commonErrors.error: Player rolls towards another defender or boundary.
commonErrors.correction: Require a scan of the exit space before turning.

commonErrors.error: Receiver turns into frontal pressure.
commonErrors.correction: Close the body and use the short-release option.

commonErrors.error: Player releases despite having open ground.
commonErrors.correction: Encourage continuation through the gate.

commonErrors.error: Football is carried on the pressure side.
commonErrors.correction: Shift it to the protected side during the movement.

progressions: Permit controlled tackling.
Add a second pressure player.
Remove the marked gates.
Add multiple support targets.
Continue into live 2v2 play.
regressions: Tell the receiver where pressure begins.
Practise one movement option at a time.
matchApplication: Players receiving through half-back, midfield or around stoppage must decide instantly whether to maintain momentum, evade pressure or move the football before being tackled.

title: Inside Runner or Outside Runner
primarySkill: Selecting the most effective running support lane
objective: Teach supporting players to choose an inside or outside running lane that complements the ball carrier and creates the greatest attacking advantage.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Use three attackers against two defenders.
One attacker begins as the ball carrier.
Two supporting runners begin behind and to either side.
Mark an inside gate near the corridor and an outside gate near the boundary.
Defenders vary their width and closing positions.
howTheDrillWorks:
The ball carrier advances towards the defenders.
Supporting runners scan the defensive shape and each other.
One runner selects the inside lane and the other holds outside width.
If the defenders compress centrally, the outside runner becomes the preferred option.
If defenders spread wide, the inside runner attacks the central gap.
The ball carrier draws a defender before releasing.
Attackers attempt to exit through either gate.
Two points are awarded for using the lane that best exploits the defensive shape.
Defenders counterattack after turnover.
Rotate all positions.
coachingPoints: Runners must occupy different lanes.
Hold outside width when central defenders compress.
Attack the inside gap when defenders separate.
Time the run so the ball carrier can draw pressure first.
Avoid crossing directly in front of another runner.
Communicate the selected lane.
Maintain defensive balance behind the play.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether runners select complementary lanes.
Whether the defensive shape is recognised.
Whether the preferred option changes correctly.
Whether runs begin too early.
Whether the ball carrier commits a defender.
Whether width and depth are maintained.

commonErrors.error: Both runners use the same lane.
commonErrors.correction: Allocate initial inside and outside roles, then allow live swapping.

commonErrors.error: Outside runner drifts towards the football.
commonErrors.correction: Mark a minimum-width channel.

commonErrors.error: Inside runner enters a congested corridor.
commonErrors.correction: Require a scan of defender spacing before accelerating.

commonErrors.error: Ball carrier releases before drawing pressure.
commonErrors.correction: Set a release line that must be reached first.

commonErrors.error: Runners cross and block one another.
commonErrors.correction: Use staggered depth and clearer communication.

progressions: Add a third defender.
Remove the marked gates.
Add a trailing support player.
Continue through a second phase.
Increase contact to match intensity.
successIndicators: Select the lane offering the strongest advantage.
matchApplication: Inside and outside runners help teams move through defensive lines. Their value depends on reading defender spacing and creating complementary rather than duplicated movement.

title: Decision-Making Movement Phase Assessment
primarySkill: Integrated movement decision making under match-like pressure
objective: Assess players’ ability to coordinate movement before, during and after possession across the complete Decision Making movement-development phase.
groundSize: Half to three-quarter ground divided into defensive exit, midfield movement and forward-entry zones.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert scenarios with multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Divide the playing area into three connected zones.
The defensive zone contains boundary, corridor and reset exits.
The midfield zone requires coordinated support, overlap and lane selection.
The forward zone contains leading, holding, clearing and late-run opportunities.
Use two balanced teams.
Position spare footballs around the area for rapid restarts.
Assign coaches or player leaders to record movement decisions.
howTheDrillWorks:
One team begins with possession in the defensive zone.
Players organise support ahead of and behind the football.
On entering midfield, players choose between carrying, releasing, overlapping, folding or holding shape.
Forward players coordinate early leads, decoy movement, clearing runs and late arrivals.
The attacking team scores three points for a goal or successful target entry.
One additional point is awarded for each clearly correct movement decision identified by the assessor.
The defending team scores for turnovers and successful counterattacks.
On turnover, both teams immediately reorganise into attacking and defensive lanes.
Coaches restart from different zones to vary the movement problem.
Play in four-minute blocks with one-minute review periods.
Rotate players through defensive, midfield and forward roles.
Complete at least four blocks before final assessment.
coachingPoints: Scan before moving and before receiving.
Decide whether to lead, hold, clear, overlap, fold or rotate.
Maintain separate lanes around possession.
Keep at least one player connected behind the football.
Use decoy and late movement to manipulate defenders.
Select inside or outside lanes according to defensive shape.
Replace positions vacated by teammates.
React immediately after turnovers.
Assess movement decisions separately from execution errors.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether movement begins after scanning.
Whether leading patterns remain coordinated.
Whether players select safe receiving paths.
Whether overlaps create genuine advantage.
Whether support remains ahead and behind possession.
Whether decoy and late runs affect defenders.
Whether players rotate into vacated positions.
Whether teams retain width and depth.
Whether transition lanes are filled quickly.
Whether decision quality survives fatigue and pressure.

commonErrors.error: Players follow fixed running patterns regardless of the picture.
commonErrors.correction: Change defender positions and restart locations regularly.

commonErrors.error: Too many players move towards the football.
commonErrors.correction: Score width, depth and clearing movement.

commonErrors.error: Teams lose all support behind possession.
commonErrors.correction: Require one player to hold defensive balance.

commonErrors.error: Early leads remain in the space and block late runners.
commonErrors.correction: Continue through the zone and clear fully.

commonErrors.error: Players fail to replace vacated positions.
commonErrors.correction: Use brief freeze-and-question reviews between blocks.

commonErrors.error: Coaches judge only disposal outcomes.
commonErrors.correction: Record movement decision and execution as separate measures.

progressions: Remove all marked zones and gates.
Increase pressure to full match intensity.
Add scoreboard and time scenarios.
Begin from stoppages, kick-ins and intercepted marks.
Require player leaders to organise movement.
Record individual results across repeated sessions.
regressions: Assess one zone at a time.
Allocate one movement focus to each line.
Pause after selected possessions for guided questioning.
successIndicators: Coordinate leads, holds and clearing runs.
Select effective inside and outside lanes.
Use decoy and late movement purposefully.
Explain how their movement created or protected team advantage.
matchApplication: The assessment recreates the connected movement demands of Australian football from defensive exit through midfield progression and forward entry. It evaluates whether players can adapt their positioning and running patterns to the live game picture rather than relying on predetermined movement.

title: Front-and-Centre Action Choice
primarySkill: Selecting the first action after front-and-centre possession
objective: Teach front-and-centre players to decide whether to take possession, release immediately, snap at goal, gain territory or protect the football after an aerial contest.
groundSize: A 25 × 30-metre area with goals or three target gates.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Position one attacker and one defender in an aerial contest.
Place one front-and-centre attacker and one defensive-side opponent at ground level.
Position one supporting attacker outside the contest.
Set goals or target gates ahead.
A kicker sends the football into the aerial contest.
Vary the contest location so the front-and-centre player experiences different field positions.
howTheDrillWorks:
The kicker sends a high football to the aerial contest.
The front-and-centre player times movement towards the likely drop zone.
If the football spills, the player scans pressure, goal location and support.
With time near goal, the player may take possession and snap or kick.
Under immediate pressure, the player may release to outside support.
If clean possession is unsafe, the player may knock or soccer the football towards team advantage.
The defensive-side opponent attempts to pressure or win the spill.
Two points are awarded for the correct first action.
A successful score or team exit adds one point.
Rotate all roles after several repetitions.
coachingPoints: Arrive at the contest moving rather than waiting underneath it.
Read the likely spoil direction.
Know the goal and boundary location before collecting.
Take clean possession when balance and time permit.
Use support when pressure arrives immediately.
Snap or kick only when the scoring opportunity is realistic.
Knock or soccer the football purposefully when possession is unsafe.
Continue after the first action.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Timing of the front-and-centre run.
Whether the likely drop zone is recognised.
Whether the player scans before taking possession.
Whether scoring attempts suit the available time and angle.
Whether support is used under pressure.
Whether emergency knocks or kicks create team advantage.
Whether defensive-side coverage is maintained.

commonErrors.error: Player stands beneath the aerial contest.
commonErrors.correction: Begin deeper and arrive as the football reaches the contest.

commonErrors.error: Player takes possession despite immediate frontal pressure.
commonErrors.correction: Use a quick release or controlled knock to support.

commonErrors.error: Player snaps at goal from a poor angle with teammates free.
commonErrors.correction: Scan goal, pressure and support before deciding.

commonErrors.error: Front-and-centre player overruns the drop zone.
commonErrors.correction: Adjust starting depth and arrival speed.

commonErrors.error: Outside support enters the contest and removes the release.
commonErrors.correction: Hold a clear passing angle outside congestion.

progressions: Add a second ground-level defender.
Use full legal aerial and ground-level pressure.
Remove marked starting positions.
Continue into live forward-50 play.
Add scoreboard and time scenarios.
Vary the kick direction and spoil type.
regressions: Roll the football from the aerial contest.
successIndicators: Avoid low-percentage possession or scoring attempts.
matchApplication: Front-and-centre players can create scores or prevent defensive exits, but only when the first action matches the spill, pressure and field position. The best decision may be possession, release, territory or an immediate shot.

title: Pressure and Contest Phase Assessment
primarySkill: Integrated decision making through pressure and contested phases
objective: Assess players’ ability to gather information, select effective actions and maintain team structure across varied pressure, contest and transition situations.
groundSize: Half to three-quarter ground divided into four connected assessment zones.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert scenarios with multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Create four connected assessment zones:
Zone 1 – Contest and First Release: Begin with a stoppage, ground ball or aerial spill.
Zone 2 – Pressure Escape: Players respond to boundary pressure, a trap or a blocked disposal lane.
Zone 3 – Transition Choice: The possession team selects corridor, width or reset according to the defensive shape.
Zone 4 – Attacking Outcome: Players respond to an aerial contest, front-and-centre spill or turnover near goal.
Use two balanced teams. Position coaches or player leaders around the ground to record decision quality and execution separately.
howTheDrillWorks:
The coach begins each passage with a contested football in Zone 1.
Players decide whether to possess, tap, protect or release.
The team winning possession attempts to exit through Zone 2.
Defenders apply one of several pressure problems, including a boundary trap, converging pressure or a smothered lane.
In Zone 3, attackers assess whether to use the corridor, switch wide or reset possession.
Zone 4 ends with a forward entry, aerial contest, front-and-centre opportunity or scoring attempt.
Each clearly correct decision scores one assessment point.
Successful execution scores a separate point.
A goal or completed target entry scores three team points.
A turnover followed by a successful counterattack scores three points for the opposition.
Coaches vary the starting contest and pressure problem on every passage.
Play in four-minute blocks with one-minute review periods.
Rotate players through inside, outside, defensive and attacking roles.
Complete at least five blocks before final assessment.
coachingPoints: Scan opponents, teammates, space and field position before possession.
Select possession only when it creates control.
Use support rather than attempting to escape every contest individually.
Recognise the boundary, corridor and turnover consequence.
Reassess when a disposal lane closes.
Maintain complementary ground-level roles around aerial contests.
Adapt stoppage exits when the planned side is pressured.
Spread only after possession becomes stable.
Keep support behind the football during transition.
React immediately to turnovers, spills and deflections.
Judge the decision separately from the execution result.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether players scan before contests and receives.
Whether possession, knock and protection decisions suit the pressure.
Whether the first release moves away from congestion.
Whether players recognise boundary and corridor risks.
Whether traps and blocked lanes are identified early.
Whether aerial-contest ground-level roles remain balanced.
Whether stoppage exits adapt to the opposition shape.
Whether players spread at the correct time.
Whether transition maintains width, depth and rear support.
Whether teams counter-pressure immediately.
Whether decision quality is maintained under fatigue and contact.
Whether players can explain the reasoning behind their choices.

commonErrors.error: Players focus only on winning the initial contest.
commonErrors.correction: Score the first release and transition decision separately.

commonErrors.error: Ball winners attempt to escape without using support.
commonErrors.correction: Require visible lateral or rear options around the contest.

commonErrors.error: Players continue with the original plan after pressure changes.
commonErrors.correction: Use guided questions about what changed in the picture.

commonErrors.error: Too many teammates enter congestion.
commonErrors.correction: Reinforce nearest, support and spread roles.

commonErrors.error: Teams attack the corridor regardless of defensive coverage.
commonErrors.correction: Reward correct wide or reset decisions.

commonErrors.error: Players stop following a spill, deflection or turnover.
commonErrors.correction: Continue scoring through the next phase of play.

commonErrors.error: Coaches assess only successful disposals.
commonErrors.correction: Maintain separate decision and execution scores.

progressions: Increase contact to full legal match intensity.
Remove all marked zones and gates.
Add scoreboard, time and field-position scenarios.
Begin from boundary throw-ins, kick-ins, centre bounces and intercepted marks.
Require player leaders to organise exits and transition.
Extend the activity to full-ground dimensions.
Record individual decision profiles across repeated sessions.
regressions: Assess one zone at a time.
Give each player one specific decision focus.
Use controlled football feeds rather than live contests.
successIndicators: Connect contest wins to organised transition.
Explain why their decisions suited the game picture.
matchApplication: This assessment connects the major pressure and contest problems players face in Australian football. It measures whether they can win or recover possession, escape pressure, reorganise support and transition into attack without losing awareness of turnover risk, field position or team structure.

title: Kick-In Shape Decision
objective: Teach players to select and execute an appropriate kick-in method according to the opposition press, teammate positioning and available continuation options.
groundSize: From the goal square to the centre square.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert scenarios with multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Use a full defensive kick-in structure.
Position the opposition in varied presses:
High man-on-man.
Central zone.
Boundary-side press.
Loose full-ground zone.
Mark short pockets, central release areas, switch zones and long-kick contest zones.
Require the possession team to organise ground-level support around any long target.
Rotate the kick-in player regularly.
howTheDrillWorks:
The kick-in player scans the opposition press before bringing the football into play.
Teammates establish short, wide, central and long options.
Against an unguarded short option, the kicker may release quickly.
Against a boundary-side press, the team may switch through the opposite pocket or central release.
Against a high press, the team may use movement behind defenders or a structured long kick.
A kick-in exit beyond defensive 50 scores two points.
A clean exit that directly exploits the press scores an additional point.
A turnover inside defensive 50 gives the opposition three points.
Play continues until possession reaches midfield, a turnover occurs or the football leaves the area.
Change the press before each restart.
coachingPoints: Identify the press before deciding the kick-in method.
Short possession is useful only when the receiver has continuation.
Use movement to create separation rather than standing at fixed cones.
Maintain weak-side width.
Long kicks require aerial and ground-level structure.
Avoid kicking to a contest where the opposition has numerical advantage.
Use the full protected area where competition rules permit.
Communicate the selected exit shape quickly.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the kicker scans the complete setup.
Whether short options have a viable next disposal.
Whether player movement creates separation.
Whether weak-side width remains available.
Whether long targets have appropriate support.
Whether the exit method suits the press.
Whether players react after a turnover.
Whether the kicker delays until the press is fully set when an earlier option existed.

commonErrors.error: Kicker selects the preferred side before scanning.
commonErrors.correction: Require identification of the press before bringing the football into play.

commonErrors.error: Short receiver is trapped immediately.
commonErrors.correction: Ensure the receiver has a second option or space to play on.

commonErrors.error: Long kick goes to an outnumbered contest.
commonErrors.correction: Count aerial and ground-level numbers before disposal.

commonErrors.error: Weak-side players move towards the ball too early.
commonErrors.correction: Hold width until the kick-in direction is confirmed.

commonErrors.error: Teammates remain stationary.
commonErrors.correction: Use coordinated leads, rotations and clearing movement.

progressions: Remove marked zones.
Allow the opposition to change press during the kick-in.
Add scoreboard and time pressure.
Increase defensive pressure to match intensity.
Continue into full-ground transition.
Require player leaders to organise the setup without coach direction.
regressions: Tell the possession team which press will be used.
Use one kick-in method at a time.
Begin with a free short option.
Reduce the distance required for a successful exit.
successIndicators: Create short, long, central and switch options.
Exit defensive 50 without unnecessary turnover risk.
matchApplication: Kick-ins provide structured possession but are immediately challenged by organised defensive presses. Players must select the exit method that best matches the opposition shape rather than relying on one rehearsed pattern.

title: Look-Off and Release
objective: Teach players to hold or redirect a defender’s attention before releasing the football to a receiver outside the defender’s immediate focus.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Position one ball carrier in the centre.
Place four receivers around the outside of the area.
Position two defenders between the ball carrier and the receivers.
One defender protects the forward half and one protects the lateral or rear half.
Receivers may move within short target zones.
A feeder supplies the ball carrier from behind or from the side.
howTheDrillWorks:
The ball carrier scans all four receivers before possession.
The feeder delivers the football.
Defenders track the ball carrier’s head, shoulders and football position.
The ball carrier looks towards one receiver long enough to hold or shift a defender.
Without losing balance, the player releases to another receiver whose lane has opened.
The receiver continues possession to a second target.
Two points are awarded when the look-off clearly creates the passing lane.
One point is awarded for a correct direct release when deception is unnecessary.
Defenders score for an intercept or for forcing the ball carrier to hold beyond three seconds.
Rotate all roles after several repetitions.
coachingPoints: Use peripheral vision to retain awareness of the intended target.
Look off the defender, not the teammate.
Keep the disposal action compact and repeatable.
Do not stare at the false option so long that the real target closes.
Recognise defenders who refuse to follow the eyes.
Use a direct disposal when the best lane is already open.
Receivers must continue moving and remain available.
Follow the disposal to provide the next support option.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the player scans before receiving.
Whether the defender’s attention is manipulated.
Whether the intended target remains visible peripherally.
Whether the disposal is accurate despite the player looking elsewhere.
Whether receivers maintain movement.
Whether players use deception unnecessarily.
Whether defenders learn to remain balanced.

commonErrors.error: Player loses awareness of the real target.
commonErrors.correction: Complete the full scan before beginning the look-off.

commonErrors.error: Disposal becomes inaccurate because the player’s body faces away.
commonErrors.correction: Keep the hips and feet balanced towards the likely release area.

commonErrors.error: Look-off lasts too long.
commonErrors.correction: Release on the defender’s first clear shift.

commonErrors.error: Player uses the same false target every repetition.
commonErrors.correction: Vary the look direction and intended receiver.

commonErrors.error: Receiver stops moving while waiting.
commonErrors.correction: Continue adjusting the passing angle until the football is released.

progressions: Permit defenders to intercept at full speed.
Add a third defender.
Remove the three-second possession limit but increase physical pressure.
Allow receivers to rotate positions during the play.
Require a disguised kick to one target and a disguised handball to another.
Continue into a live possession game.
regressions: Predetermine the false and real targets.
Allow the player to begin with possession.
successIndicators: Retain awareness of the intended target.
Release at the moment the lane opens.
Use direct options when deception is not required.
matchApplication: Looking off a defender can open central handball lanes, create forward entries and prevent opponents from leaving their direct opponent early. The action is most valuable when it changes the defender’s decision without delaying possession.

title: Delayed Disposal Window
objective: Teach players to recognise when an immediate disposal would waste an emerging advantage and when delaying briefly will create a better release option.
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Position one ball carrier at the base of the area.
Place two supporting attackers ahead and one behind.
Position two defenders between the carrier and forward targets.
One supporting attacker begins moving immediately.
The second enters late from a delayed starting cone.
The defenders decide whether to press the carrier, hold the first target or track the late runner.
howTheDrillWorks:
The ball carrier receives and scans the first available options.
The early support player presents immediately.
The late runner enters after a one- to two-second delay.
If the early target has clear advantage, the ball carrier releases immediately.
If defenders remain balanced and the late runner is likely to create the spare, the carrier protects possession briefly.
The ball carrier releases as soon as a defender commits or the delayed option enters advantage.
Holding beyond the useful window allows defenders to close all options.
Two points are awarded for a correctly timed delayed release.
One point is awarded for a correct immediate disposal.
Defenders score for trapping the carrier or forcing an ineffective delay.
coachingPoints: Delay only when a better option is actively developing.
Protect the football and remain balanced while waiting.
Do not hold possession simply because a late runner exists.
Release immediately when the first option already has advantage.
Watch defender commitment rather than counting a fixed number of seconds.
Use small foot movements to maintain space and disposal angle.
Support players must time movement precisely.
Avoid delaying until the disposal window closes.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether the player distinguishes between useful and unnecessary delay.
Whether possession remains protected.
Whether defenders are manipulated by the hold.
Whether the late runner creates genuine advantage.
Whether immediate options are ignored.
Whether the final release occurs before pressure arrives.
Whether support movement is properly timed.

commonErrors.error: Ball carrier always waits for the late runner.
commonErrors.correction: Use the first option whenever it already has clear advantage.

commonErrors.error: Player disposes immediately before the defence commits.
commonErrors.correction: Hold briefly when the developing movement can create a spare.

commonErrors.error: Delay becomes static possession.
commonErrors.correction: Maintain active feet and change the disposal angle.

commonErrors.error: Player holds until tackled.
commonErrors.correction: Release on the defender’s first decisive commitment.

commonErrors.error: Late runner enters before the defence is engaged.
commonErrors.correction: Delay behind the starting cone until the carrier attracts attention.

progressions: Add controlled tackling pressure.
Introduce two late runners from different directions.
Remove the delayed starting cone.
Allow defenders to disguise their intended commitment.
Add scoreboard consequences for turnovers.
Continue into a live 4v3 transition.
regressions: Predetermine whether the early or late option will be best.
Increase the starting distance of pressure.
successIndicators: Recognise when immediate disposal is best.
Hold possession only while advantage develops.
matchApplication: Some advantages appear only after a defender commits or a late runner arrives. Elite decision makers can hold possession briefly without becoming trapped, allowing the team’s movement to create a stronger option.

title: Numerical Bait and Switch
primarySkill: Drawing defenders before transferring to the spare side
objective: Teach players to attract defensive numbers towards one area before transferring possession to a genuine spare player or open side.
groundSize: 40 × 50 metres divided into ball-side, corridor and weak-side channels.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert scenarios with multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Use six to twelve attackers against five to eleven defenders.
Begin possession in one outside channel.
Position two or three attackers close enough to combine on the ball side.
Place at least two attackers on the weak side.
Defenders may remain balanced or compress towards repeated ball-side possession.
Mark a scoring gate at the end of each outside channel.
Require one attacker to remain behind possession as the switching outlet.
howTheDrillWorks:
Attackers begin with one or two controlled disposals on the ball side.
The team scans whether defenders are being drawn towards the repeated possession.
If defenders compress, the rear outlet receives and initiates the switch.
Weak-side players hold width until the football begins transferring.
The switch may travel through the corridor, a rear player or a two-player chain.
If defenders refuse to compress, attackers may continue through the original side.
A successful weak-side gate entry after drawing three or more defenders scores three points.
A successful ball-side entry against balanced defence scores one point.
An intercepted transfer scores two points for defenders.
Teams reverse direction after turnovers.
coachingPoints: Ball-side possession must be credible enough to attract defenders.
Do not hold or overuse the football once compression has occurred.
Scan the weak side before the transfer begins.
Keep the rear outlet at sufficient depth.
Weak-side players must preserve width.
Transfer quickly enough to beat defensive recovery.
Continue on the original side when defenders do not commit.
Maintain turnover protection during the switch.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether ball-side possession attracts defenders.
Whether players recognise the moment of compression.
Whether the rear outlet remains available.
Whether weak-side width is maintained.
Whether the transfer is safe and fast.
Whether teams switch without first moving the defence.
Whether the original side is used when still advantageous.
Whether intercept risk is assessed.

commonErrors.error: Team switches before defenders have compressed.
commonErrors.correction: Complete credible ball-side possession and reassess the numbers.

commonErrors.error: Ball-side players continue combining after the spare side appears.
commonErrors.correction: Transfer immediately once the defensive shift creates advantage.

commonErrors.error: Weak-side players move towards the football.
commonErrors.correction: Hold position beyond the minimum-width line.

commonErrors.error: Rear outlet is too flat and easily pressured.
commonErrors.correction: Create greater depth and a safer angle behind possession.

commonErrors.error: Cross-ground disposal travels through a crowded corridor.
commonErrors.correction: Use an additional connector or a safer rear transfer.

progressions: Remove channel markings.
Allow defenders to disguise their compression.
Add full transition after interception.
Require a switch through two different disposal types.
Add scoreboard and time scenarios.
Extend across full-ground dimensions.
regressions: Begin with a clear weak-side numerical advantage.
Allow the coach to call the switch.
successIndicators: Exploit the spare side with controlled possession.
matchApplication: Teams can create space away from the football by attracting defenders through credible possession. The switch becomes valuable only after the opposition has committed enough numbers to create a genuine spare side.

title: Leadership Call and Player Override
primarySkill: Responding intelligently to tactical leadership calls
objective: Teach players to follow clear leadership calls when they suit the game picture while retaining responsibility to override or modify the call when immediate information makes it unsafe or ineffective.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert scenarios with multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Divide players into two balanced teams.
Nominate a captain and one line leader for each team.
Establish several simple calls, such as:
Switch.
Control.
Fast.
Boundary.
Corridor.
Hold.
Begin each passage from a different field position.
The opposition may change its shape after the leadership call.
Leaders cannot cancel or modify the call after the ball carrier begins the action.
howTheDrillWorks:
A team begins with possession.
The captain or line leader makes a tactical call.
Players begin reorganising according to the call.
The opposition then adjusts its shape or pressure.
Ball carriers and nearby players must determine whether the original call remains appropriate.
When the call remains suitable, the team executes it collectively.
When immediate pressure makes it unsafe, the ball carrier may override or modify the action.
Two points are awarded for correctly executing a suitable leadership call.
Two points are also awarded for a justified override that preserves or improves possession.
An unjustified override or blind obedience that causes a turnover gives the opposition two points.
Review the reasoning between passages.
Rotate leadership roles regularly.
coachingPoints: Leadership calls provide a shared method, not an excuse to ignore live information.
Players should follow the call unless a clear immediate reason prevents it.
Overrides must be based on pressure, lane closure, numbers or field position.
Communicate the override quickly so teammates can adjust.
Avoid changing the method because of personal preference.
Leaders should make early, simple and specific calls.
Players remain accountable for the final action.
Review whether the call or execution caused the outcome.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether leadership calls are early and clear.
Whether players reorganise collectively.
Whether the live game picture is visually confirmed.
Whether overrides are justified.
Whether players ignore calls without a clear reason.
Whether players follow instructions into obvious pressure.
Whether the team adjusts quickly after an override.
Whether leaders accept and review player decisions.

commonErrors.error: Player follows a call into a closed lane.
commonErrors.correction: Confirm the current pressure and passing lane before execution.

commonErrors.error: Player ignores the call because another option is preferred.
commonErrors.correction: Override only when the original method is genuinely unsafe or unavailable.

commonErrors.error: Override occurs without teammate communication.
commonErrors.correction: Use a clear call such as “hold”, “change” or “reset”.

commonErrors.error: Leader makes the call after possession is already pressured.
commonErrors.correction: Communicate before the ball carrier must act.

commonErrors.error: Team blames execution failure on the tactical call.
commonErrors.correction: Separate the quality of the call from the quality of the skill execution.

progressions: Conceal the opposition adjustment from team leaders.
Require captain-only tactical calls.
Change score and time during passages.
Increase pressure to full match intensity.
Use full-ground practice-match conditions.
Record leadership and override decisions for video review.
regressions: Tell players when an override will be required.
Allow coaches to support the leader.
successIndicators: Confirm the call against live information.
Override only for clear tactical reasons.
Accept responsibility for the final decision.
matchApplication: Players must respond to captains, line leaders and team calls while still reading the immediate game picture. Effective teams combine collective tactical direction with individual responsibility at the moment of action.

title: Defensive Mismatch Protection
objective: Teach defenders to recognise an unfavourable match-up and decide whether to switch, provide help, protect space or increase pressure on the ball carrier.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert scenarios with multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Use six to twelve attackers against six to twelve defenders.
Create an unfavourable defensive match-up inside forward 50.
Position one potential help defender and one last-line defender nearby.
Begin the attacking possession 50–70 metres from goal.
Vary whether pressure can be applied to the ball carrier.
Defenders are not told in advance whether switching, helping or holding shape will be best.
howTheDrillWorks:
The attacking team gains possession outside forward 50.
Defenders scan match-ups and identify the primary danger.
The direct defender communicates whether help or a switch is needed.
If a safe handover is available, defenders may switch opponents.
If switching would release another dangerous target, a help defender protects the likely disposal space.
When help positioning leaves another option exposed, teammates increase pressure on the ball carrier.
Defenders score one point for preventing the mismatch from receiving cleanly.
Winning possession and exiting defensive 50 scores two additional points.
Attackers score three points for a goal created through the mismatch.
Rotate match-ups and help-defender roles.
coachingPoints: Identify the most dangerous mismatch early.
Communicate before the forward movement begins.
Switch only when responsibilities are clearly transferred.
Help from a position that still allows recovery.
Increase pressure on the ball carrier when defensive coverage is vulnerable.
Avoid sending multiple defenders to the same opponent.
Maintain last-line protection.
Rebound with control after winning possession.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether defenders identify the mismatch.
Whether communication occurs early.
Whether switches are completed safely.
Whether help defenders protect the likely space.
Whether another dangerous attacker is released.
Whether pressure on the ball carrier improves.
Whether last-line protection remains.
Whether rebound decisions are controlled.

commonErrors.error: Defenders recognise the mismatch but do not communicate.
commonErrors.correction: Use an early, specific call identifying the opponent and required help.

commonErrors.error: Help defender commits fully and leaves another attacker free.
commonErrors.correction: Position to influence the mismatch while retaining recovery ability.

commonErrors.error: Two defenders switch without confirming responsibilities.
commonErrors.correction: Complete a clear verbal and visual handover.

commonErrors.error: Defenders focus only on the target and allow an unpressured entry.
commonErrors.correction: Increase pressure on the ball carrier to reduce disposal quality.

commonErrors.error: All defenders collapse and leave no rebound outlet.
commonErrors.correction: Maintain one defender or outside player in a release position.

progressions: Allow attackers to rotate and create new mismatches.
Remove designated help defenders.
Increase pressure to match intensity.
Begin from turnovers and repeat entries.
Add scoreboard and time scenarios.
Require player leaders to organise all defensive adjustments.
regressions: Predetermine whether to switch or help.
Reduce the number of attacking targets.
successIndicators: Maintain coverage of other dangerous options.
Apply pressure to the ball carrier.
matchApplication: Defensive match-ups change through rotations, injuries, transition and opposition tactics. Teams must recognise when help or switching is required without creating a larger problem elsewhere.

title: Weather-Adjusted Decision Game
primarySkill: Adjusting decisions to weather and ground conditions
objective: Develop players’ ability to adjust disposal type, possession method, field positioning and risk according to wind, rain, slippery ground or reduced visibility.
equipment: Water spray for footballs where safe
coachingDifficulty: 4 – Advanced tactical coaching, live constraints and active correction
setup:
Use two balanced teams.
Prepare safe scenario conditions representing:
Strong wind towards one end.
Crosswind.
Wet or slippery football.
Slower ground movement.
Reduced marking reliability.
Do not create unsafe footing or uncontrolled wet surfaces.
Mark territory gates, short-possession zones and ground-level support areas.
Begin from varied field positions.
howTheDrillWorks:
The coach announces or introduces the current weather condition.
Teams play towards the scoring end under normal football rules.
Players adjust disposal type, target location and possession method.
Into strong wind, teams may use lower disposals, shorter connections and running support.
With the wind, players judge carry distance and avoid overkicking targets.
In slippery conditions, players anticipate spills and increase ground-level support.
A decision suited to the condition scores one point.
Successful execution scores a separate point.
Unsafe or unrealistic disposal choices give the opposition one point.
Change the condition every three to four minutes.
coachingPoints: Adjust the decision before blaming execution.
Keep kicks lower and more direct into strong wind.
Allow for extra carry with the wind.
Use wider safety margins in a crosswind.
Expect marks and pickups to spill in wet conditions.
Maintain additional ground-level support.
Use territory when clean possession is difficult.
Avoid high-risk central disposals when conditions reduce control.
Protect player safety on slippery ground.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether disposal choices change with conditions.
Whether players adjust kick height and direction.
Whether ground-level support increases.
Whether players continue attempting dry-weather skills in slippery conditions.
Whether territory is used intelligently.
Whether central turnover risk is understood.
Whether players communicate wind and ground information.
Whether movement remains safe.

commonErrors.error: Players use the same disposal method in every condition.
commonErrors.correction: Identify how wind or moisture changes flight, bounce and control.

commonErrors.error: High kicks are used into strong wind.
commonErrors.correction: Use lower, more penetrating disposals and running support.

commonErrors.error: Players stand for marks in wet conditions without ground support.
commonErrors.correction: Position teammates front and centre and defensive side.

commonErrors.error: With-wind kicks travel beyond the target.
commonErrors.correction: Reduce force and allow for additional carry.

commonErrors.error: Players take unnecessary central risk on a slippery football.
commonErrors.correction: Use safer territory and visible support options.

progressions: Change conditions without announcing them.
Add scoreboard and time scenarios.
Increase pressure to match intensity.
Use opposing conditions in each half.
Allow player leaders to establish the method.
Continue into a full practice match.
regressions: Work with one condition at a time.
successIndicators: Adjust disposal height, distance and direction.
matchApplication: Weather and ground conditions change the probability and consequence of decisions. Successful teams adapt their method rather than attempting to play identical football regardless of wind, rain or surface quality.

title: Fatigue Decision Integrity
objective: Develop players’ ability to preserve scanning, option selection and team structure as physical fatigue increases.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert scenarios with multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Use two teams of six to twelve players.
Position a scoring gate at each end.
Play repeated high-intensity blocks of 60–90 seconds.
Provide short recovery periods.
Require at least one forward, one lateral and one rear support option.
Record decision quality during the first and final 20 seconds of each block.
Adjust work-to-rest ratios for age, fitness and playing level.
howTheDrillWorks:
Teams play continuously towards opposite scoring gates.
The coach begins with a contested or transition restart.
Players attempt to maintain scanning and support structure throughout the block.
A correct decision scores one assessment point.
Successful execution scores a separate point.
A rushed disposal, missed scan or structural collapse is recorded.
At the whistle, players recover briefly and receive one coaching question.
Repeat for four to six blocks.
Compare early-block and late-block decision quality.
Reduce workload immediately if technique or player safety deteriorates excessively.
coachingPoints: Continue scanning when breathing and movement become difficult.
Use simple, high-percentage options when skill control reduces.
Avoid confusing fatigue with urgency.
Maintain support behind the football.
Communicate clearly and early.
Reset mentally after errors.
Use body balance before disposal.
Recognise when the team needs controlled possession to recover structure.
Protect decision quality rather than chasing maximum physical output.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Whether scanning decreases late in blocks.
Whether players rush disposal.
Whether support becomes flat or disappears.
Whether communication reduces.
Whether players force high-risk actions.
Whether errors cause further poor decisions.
Whether physical load remains appropriate.
Whether decision quality improves across repeated blocks.

commonErrors.error: Players stop scanning when fatigued.
commonErrors.correction: Use a visible head-check requirement before receiving.

commonErrors.error: Disposal becomes rushed and unbalanced.
commonErrors.correction: Secure body position before selecting the action.

commonErrors.error: Team loses rear support.
commonErrors.correction: Nominate and communicate one connected player behind possession.

commonErrors.error: Fatigued players attempt increasingly difficult options.
commonErrors.correction: Use simpler possession until control and structure improve.

commonErrors.error: Players mentally disengage after an error.
commonErrors.correction: Focus immediately on the next role and decision.

progressions: Increase block length gradually.
Reduce recovery periods.
Add scoreboard and time scenarios.
Begin each block from a different match phase.
Increase pressure to full match intensity.
Track individual decision accuracy under fatigue.
regressions: Limit the number of consecutive repetitions for Over 35 players.
successIndicators: Select options suited to declining control.
Limit the decline in decision quality.
matchApplication: Many decisive moments occur late in quarters and matches when players are fatigued. Teams that preserve scanning, structure and risk control are less likely to concede damaging turnovers.

title: Unscripted Chaos Match
primarySkill: Adapting to unpredictable match events without coach direction
objective: Develop players’ ability to independently solve unpredictable game problems while maintaining team structure, communication and decision quality.
groundSize: Full ground preferred; three-quarter ground minimum.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert scenarios with multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Divide players into two balanced teams.
Use normal positional structures.
Prepare hidden event cards including:
Sudden numerical advantage or disadvantage.
Change of defensive press.
Strong wind direction.
Scoreboard change.
Umpire-call sequence.
Injured-player simulation requiring positional rotation.
Wet-football period.
Reduced time remaining.
Opposition tactical switch.
Assign captains and line leaders.
Coaches introduce events without prescribing the response.
howTheDrillWorks:
Teams begin a normal practice match.
Every two to four minutes, the coach introduces an unscripted event.
Players must identify what changed and determine the response.
Captains and line leaders communicate any tactical adjustment.
Coaches do not provide the solution during live play.
One assessment point is awarded when a team recognises the event and responds effectively.
A second point is awarded when the response is coordinated across all lines.
Normal match scoring continues.
Repeated failure to adapt allows the opposition to retain the tactical advantage.
Play continues through turnovers, scores and restarts.
Complete six to eight event changes.
Finish with a player-led review before coach feedback.
coachingPoints: Identify the changed variable before altering team behaviour.
Maintain core principles while adapting the specific method.
Communicate information quickly across the ground.
Avoid waiting for coach direction.
Use leaders without removing individual responsibility.
Reassess whether the response is working.
Separate tactical failure from skill execution error.
Maintain width, depth and turnover protection.
Recover emotionally after unexpected events.
Continue making decisions while fatigued.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Speed of event recognition.
Accuracy of the team response.
Leadership communication.
Coordination between defenders, midfielders and forwards.
Whether players wait for coach instructions.
Whether unnecessary structural changes occur.
Whether the response improves the game picture.
Whether players self-correct.
Whether fatigue affects awareness.
Whether emotional responses disrupt decisions.

commonErrors.error: Players continue as though nothing changed.
commonErrors.correction: Require leaders to identify and communicate the new variable.

commonErrors.error: Team changes several unrelated elements.
commonErrors.correction: Modify only the behaviours affected by the new problem.

commonErrors.error: One line adapts while others remain unchanged.
commonErrors.correction: Confirm the adjustment through each line leader.

commonErrors.error: Players repeatedly look to coaches for answers.
commonErrors.correction: Continue play and review the player-led response afterwards.

commonErrors.error: Tactical method is abandoned after one execution error.
commonErrors.correction: Judge whether the decision remained appropriate before changing again.

progressions: Introduce two simultaneous events.
Conceal some information from selected players.
Allow teams to create tactical problems for each other.
Use full legal match intensity.
Remove formal event breaks.
Record the match for detailed decision review.
regressions: Introduce one event at a time.
Limit the number of possible tactical changes.
successIndicators: Maintain decision quality under fatigue and pressure.
matchApplication: Matches contain injuries, umpiring decisions, tactical changes, weather shifts, momentum swings and unexpected numerical situations. Players must solve these problems independently while play continues.

title: Decision Making Chapter Final Assessment
primarySkill: Complete application of Australian football decision making
objective: Assess players’ ability to gather information, select effective actions, coordinate team behaviour and adapt to changing match situations across the complete Decision Making chapter.
groundSize: Full ground preferred; three-quarter ground acceptable.
coachingDifficulty: 5 – Expert scenarios with multiple lines, tactical adaptation and player feedback
setup:
Divide players into two balanced teams.
Use full-ground positions and normal match structure.
Prepare assessment phases covering:
Pre-possession scanning.
Space and pressure recognition.
Numerical advantage.
Defensive exits.
Midfield tempo.
Forward entries.
Contested and broken play.
Turnovers and transition.
Team tactical adjustment.
Scoreboard and clock scenarios.
Leadership and player-led adaptation.
Assign coaches or trained observers to different ground areas.
Record decision quality separately from execution.
Use controlled contact suitable to the playing group.
howTheDrillWorks:
Begin with a normal match restart.
Allow an initial five-minute period of uninterrupted play to establish natural decision behaviour.
Introduce a defensive-press scenario through a kick-in or defensive possession.
Begin the next passage from a stoppage or contested football.
Introduce a numerical advantage or disadvantage during transition.
Change the defensive structure between man-on-man, zone and hybrid methods.
Include a forward-entry and repeat-entry phase.
Introduce a broken-play situation through a deflection, smother or imperfect football.
Change the score and remaining time for a final-match scenario.
Introduce one unexpected event requiring player-led adaptation.
Award one assessment point for each correct decision.
Award a separate point for successful execution.
Record team-structure decisions including width, depth, support and turnover protection.
Play in five-minute blocks with brief player-led reviews.
Rotate players through defensive, midfield and forward roles.
Complete at least six assessment blocks.
Finish with individual and team feedback based on recurring patterns rather than isolated outcomes.
coachingPoints: Scan before possession and continue scanning while moving.
Recognise teammates, opponents, space, pressure and field position.
Select options that support the next phase, not only the immediate disposal.
Adjust risk to consequence, score and time.
Coordinate leading, holding, clearing and support movement.
Protect possession through pressure and contact.
Connect contested wins to effective first release and transition.
Use corridor, boundary, switch and reset options according to the defensive shape.
Match forward entries to aerial, ground-level and positional advantage.
Recognise defensive bait, traps and hidden pressure.
Manipulate opponents only when it creates genuine advantage.
Respond to leadership calls while retaining personal decision responsibility.
Adapt to weather, fatigue, umpire calls and unexpected events.
Maintain width, depth and protection behind the football.
Judge the decision separately from execution.
whatTheCoachShouldObserve: Observe:
Pre-possession scanning habits.
Recognition of pressure distance and angle.
Selection between forward, lateral and rear options.
Use of numerical advantage.
Adjustment of body orientation.
Decisions in congestion and broken play.
Timing of release, carry and evasion.
Defensive-exit selection.
Midfield tempo control.
Forward-entry quality.
Weak-side width and support rotation.
Transition after turnovers.
Recognition of defensive methods and traps.
Scoreboard and clock awareness.
Leadership communication.
Adaptation to unexpected conditions.
Decision quality under fatigue.
Emotional response after errors.
Whether execution failure is incorrectly treated as decision failure.

commonErrors.error: Players focus only on executing the skill.
commonErrors.correction: Score scanning, recognition and option selection separately.

commonErrors.error: Decision quality collapses as pressure increases.
commonErrors.correction: Rebuild early information gathering and simplify the immediate option.

commonErrors.error: Players use fixed patterns regardless of the opposition.
commonErrors.correction: Change the defensive picture and require live reassessment.

commonErrors.error: Teams lose width, depth or rear support.
commonErrors.correction: Restore complementary movement roles around possession.

commonErrors.error: High-risk actions are selected without considering consequence.
commonErrors.correction: Identify field position, score, time and likely turnover outcome.

commonErrors.error: Players wait for coach instructions during tactical problems.
commonErrors.correction: Use captains and line leaders while preserving individual responsibility.

commonErrors.error: Execution failure causes correct decisions to be abandoned.
commonErrors.correction: Separate the tactical choice from the skill outcome.

commonErrors.error: Players stop after turnovers, umpire calls or errors.
commonErrors.correction: Reassign the next role immediately and continue the phase.

progressions: Use full legal match intensity.
Remove all coach-created structures and allow teams to create tactical problems.
Conceal score or time information from selected players.
Restrict tactical communication to captains.
Introduce simultaneous changes in score, numbers and defensive method.
Add repeated high-intensity blocks to test fatigue.
Use video and coded decision analysis.
Complete the assessment within a full practice match.
regressions: Assess one decision category at a time.
Announce the tactical problem before play.
Assign one decision focus to each player.
Use guided questioning before progressing to uninterrupted play.
successIndicators: Select options that improve the next phase.
Adjust risk to field position and match context.
Make productive contested and broken-play decisions.
Maintain team ball movement and defensive balance.
Recognise opposition structures and tactical traps.
Respond appropriately to leadership and umpire calls.
Adapt to fatigue, weather and unexpected events.
Explain the reasoning behind their decisions.
Maintain decision quality across complete match-like phases.
matchApplication: This final assessment integrates the full decision-making demands of Australian football. It measures whether players can scan, interpret, choose, execute, communicate and adapt across technical, contested, tactical and match-scenario situations while preserving team structure and responding independently to a changing game.
relatedDrills: DM-097 – Umpire Call and Advantage Decision
